documents.title: Project answer
documents.text:
We built a self-service GPU job runner for the department's machine learning teaching cluster as a final-year group project with four people from Sept 2025 to March 2026. We saw 140 students use it in the spring term and the average wait for a GPU went from about two days to under 20 minutes.

We let students submit training jobs through a small web form and the runner queued them on Kubernetes with k3s on six old lab workstations with GPUs. We used Python and FastAPI for the API, Redis for the queue, Helm charts for deploys, and Prometheus and Grafana for monitoring.

We used Kubernetes Jobs with a scheduler extender instead of Slurm because the department wanted everything in containers and we needed per-course GPU quotas.

We had jobs start dying at random in week 9, pods OOMKilled even with tiny models and it took us three days to resolve. We had the default /dev/shm in the pods at 64 MB so the PyTorch data loaders crashed. We learned to check the node's kernel log first, as dmesg showed the OOM kills straight away and we wasted two days before looking.

I found the /dev/shm problem by reading dmesg on the nodes and seeing the OOM kills. My teammate Sam wrote the Helm change that mounts a memory-backed emptyDir for each job; I tested it on two of the lab nodes. I also wrote the per-course quota check in the scheduler extender.

documents.title: Cover letter
documents.text:
Dear Graphcore hiring team,

I am applying for the Graduate Cloud Platform Engineer 2027 role at Graphcore.

I liked the infrastructure side of the project more than the machine learning side, and Graphcore builds both the hardware and the cloud platform that models run on.

We built a self-service GPU job runner for the department's machine learning teaching cluster as a final-year group project with four people from Sept 2025 to March 2026. Students submitted training jobs through a small web form and the runner queued them on Kubernetes (k3s on six old lab workstations with GPUs). We used Python and FastAPI for the API, Redis for the queue, Helm charts for deploys, Prometheus and Grafana for monitoring. We used Kubernetes Jobs with a scheduler extender instead of Slurm because the department wanted everything in containers and we needed per-course GPU quotas. I wrote the per-course quota check in the scheduler extender.

In week 9 jobs started dying at random, pods OOMKilled even with tiny models and it took three days to resolve. I read dmesg on the nodes and saw the OOM kills, which identified the /dev/shm problem. For context: The default /dev/shm in the pods was 64 MB so the PyTorch data loaders crashed, and my teammate Sam wrote the Helm change that mounts a memory-backed emptyDir with a size limit per job; I tested it on two of the lab nodes. 140 students used it in the spring term and the average wait for a GPU went from about two days on the old sign-up sheet to under 20 minutes. We learned to check the node's kernel log first, dmesg showed the OOM kills straight away and we wasted two days before looking.

Thank you for considering my application.

Kind regards, Ellie
